{{Short description|Longest distance between tree vertices}}

In [[graph theory]], the '''triameter''' is a metric [[Graph property|invariant]] that generalizes the concept of a [[Diameter (graph theory)|graph's diameter]]. It is defined as the maximum sum of pairwise [[Distance (graph theory)|distances]] between any three [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] in a [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected graph]] <math display="inline">G</math> and is denoted by
<div style="overflow-x: auto;">
<math display="block">
\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) = \max\{d(u,v) + d(v,w) + d(u,w) \mid u,v,w \in V\},
</math>
</div>
where <math display="inline">V</math> is the vertex set of <math display="inline">G</math> and <math display="inline">d(u,v)</math> is the length of the shortest [[Path (graph theory)|path]] between [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] <math display="inline">u</math> and <math display="inline">v</math>.

It extends the idea of the [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]], which captures the longest [[Path (graph theory)|path]] between any two of its [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]]. A '''triametral triple''' is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of three [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] achieving <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G)</math>.

==History==

The parameter of '''triameter''' is related to the channel [[assignment problem]]—the problem of assigning [[Frequency|frequencies]] to the [[Transmitter|transmitters]] in some optimal manner and with no [[Wave interference|interferences]]. [[Gary Chartrand|Chartrand]] et al..{{R|Chartrand2005}} introduced the concept of [[Radio coloring|radio <math display="inline">k</math>-coloring]] of a [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SimpleGraph.html simple graph] in 2005. Then (2012, 2015) sharp lower bounds on [[Radio coloring|radio <math display="inline">k</math>-chromatic number]] of [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected graphs]] were provided in terms of a newly defined parameter called '''triameter''' of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]].{{R|KolaPanigrahi2015}} {{R|SahaPanigrahi2012}} {{R|SahaPanigrahi2015}} Apart from this, the concept of '''triameter''' also finds application in metric [[Polytope|polytopes]].{{R|Laurent1996}}

In 2014, Henning and Yeo proved a [[Graffiti (program)|Graffiti]] conjecture on lower bound of [[Dominating set#Variants|total domination number]] of a [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected graph]] in terms of its '''triameter'''.{{R|HenningYeo2014}} Saha and Panigrahi denoted this parameter as <math display="inline">M</math>-value of a graph in their paper.{{R|SahaPanigrahi2015}}

The concept of '''triameter''' was first formally introduced in 2021 and studied by [https://sites.google.com/site/angsumancrypto/home A. Das]. He investigated its connections to other [[Graph property|graph parameters]] such as [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]], [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GraphRadius.html radius], [[Girth (graph theory)|girth]], and [[Dominating set|domination numbers]].{{R|Das2021}} Building on this foundation, A. Hak, S. Kozerenko and B. Oliynyk extended the study in 2022 exploring an interplay between '''triameter''' and [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] for some [[:Category:Graph families|graph families]] and establishing a tight lower bound for '''triameter''' of [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] in terms of their order and number of leaves.{{R|HakKozerenkoOliynyk2022}}

Recently, K. Jeya Daisy, S. Nihisha, and P. Jeyanthi, linked '''triameter''' to the [[ring theory]], they studied '''triameter''' of the [[zero-divisor graph]] of a [[commutative ring]] with [[identity (mathematics)|identity]].{{R|JeyaNihishaJeyanthi2025}}

==Metric properties==

The metric properties of '''triameter''' were first studied by A. Das.{{R|Das2021}} The '''triameter''' of any [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] graph <math display="inline">G</math> is tightly bounded by its [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] and [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GraphRadius.html radius] in the following way: <math display="block">\begin{aligned}
2 \mathop{\mathrm{diam}}(G) \leq &\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) \leq 3 \mathop{\mathrm{diam}}(G),\\
2 \mathop{\mathrm{rad}}(G) \leq &\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) \leq 6 \mathop{\mathrm{rad}}(G).
\end{aligned}</math>

===Bounds for trees===

[[File:Tree representing tight lower triameter bound for n=17, l=5.svg|thumb|230px|A tree ''T'' with tr(''T'') = 20 representing tight lower triameter bound for ''n''=17, ''l''=5.]]

For the [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] tighter bounds hold:{{R|Das2021}}

<math display="block">4 \mathop{\mathrm{rad}}(G) - 2 \leq \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) \leq 6 \mathop{\mathrm{rad}}(G),</math> If <math display="inline">G</math> is a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] with more than <math display="inline">2</math> leaves, then the stronger lower bound <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) \geq 4\mathop{\mathrm{rad}}(G)</math> holds. For any connected graph <math display="inline">G</math> with <math display="inline">n \geq 3</math> vertices the lower bound <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(G) \leq 2n - 2</math> takes place. Moreover, the equality holds if and only if <math display="inline">G</math> is a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] with <math display="inline">2</math> or <math display="inline">3</math> leaves.

The general tight lower bound for any given pair <math display="inline">(n, l)</math> is known.{{R|HakKozerenkoOliynyk2022}} Let <math display="inline">T</math> be a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] with <math display="inline">n\geq 4</math> vertices and <math display="inline">l\geq 3</math> leaves, then the following holds:
<div style="overflow-x: auto;">
<math display="block">
\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(T)\geq 6 \left\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{l}}+2\min\{(n-1)\bmod{l},3\}\right\rfloor.
</math>
</div>

==Diameter–triameter interplay==

The key question is whether some relationships between [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] and '''triameter''' hold for various [[:Category:Graph families|graph families]]:{{R|Das2021}} {{R|HakKozerenkoOliynyk2022}}

[[File:Triameter diameter interplay.svg|thumb|330px|The graph ''G'' has tr(''G'') = d(''u'',''v'',''w'') = 12 and diam(''G'') = d(''x'',''y'') = 5. The triametral triple ''u'', ''v'', ''w'' does not contain a diametral pair, and the diametral pair ''x'', ''y'' cannot be extended to a triametral triple.]]

<div id="TD"><b>(TD)</b> Any '''triametral triple''' in a graph contains a [[Diameter (graph theory)|diametral]] pair.</div>
<div id="DT"><b>(DT)</b> Any [[Diameter (graph theory)|diametral]] pair in a graph can be extended to a '''triametral triple'''.</div>

In fact, both [[#TD|(TD)]] and [[#DT|(DT)]] hold for [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] and [[Block graph|block graphs]]. Every pair of vertices (even not diametral) in a [[symmetric graph]] can be extended to a '''triametral triple''', which implies [[#DT|(DT)]]; however, the first property [[#TD|(TD)]] does not hold for them.

There are weaker versions of these properties:{{R|HakKozerenkoOliynyk2022}}

<div id="TD'"><b>(TD<math display="inline">'</math>)</b> Any '''triametral triple''' contains a [[Glossary of graph theory#peripheral|peripheral]] vertex.</div>
<div id="D'T"><b>(D<math display="inline">'</math>T)</b> Any [[Glossary of graph theory#peripheral|peripheral]] vertex can be extended to a '''triametral triple'''.</div>

Neither [[Modular graph|modular graphs]] nor [[Distance-hereditary graph|distance hereditary graphs]] satisfy any of these properties, even weaker versions. For [[#D'T|(D<math display="inline">'</math>T)]] counterexample see the graph on the left in the [[#tr-diam-dh-counter|figure]], in fact it is both [[Modular_graph|modular]] and [[Distance-hereditary_graph|distance hereditary]]. For [[#TD'|(TD<math display="inline">'</math>)]] the [[Distance-hereditary_graph|distance hereditary]] counterexample is the graph on the right in the [[#tr-diam-dh-counter|figure]], and for the [[Modular_graph|modular]] it is a [[complete bipartite graph]] <math display="inline">K_{2,3}</math>.

{{anchor|tr-diam-dh-counter}}
[[File:A pair of distance-hereditary graphs being a counterexample to diameter--triameter interplay.svg|thumb|330px|A pair of [[Distance-hereditary_graph|distance hereditary graphs]] being a counterexample to [[#Diameter–triameter interplay|diameter–triameter interplay]]. The triametral triple ''u'', ''v'', ''w'' of the graph on the left does not contain a peripheral vertex, while the peripheral vertex ''x'' of the graph on the right cannot be extended to a triametral triple. Both graphs are [[Distance-hereditary_graph|distance hereditary]], the graph on the left is also a [[median graph]].]]

Also, [[#TD|(TD)]] does not hold for the [[Hypercube graph|hypercubes]] and, consequently, [[Median graph|median graphs]].

==Open problems==

Several open problems regarding the triameter:

* Does [[#DT|(DT)]] hold for the [[Median graph|median graphs]]? This is an interesting question because [[Median graph|median graphs]] generalize [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] and [[Hypercube graph|hypercubes]], for which [[#DT|(DT)]] holds. A Meta-Conjecture, stated by H. Mulder {{R|Mulder2016}}, suggests that any (sensible) [[Graph property|property]] shared by [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] and [[Hypercube graph|hypercubes]] is also shared by all [[Median graph|median graphs]]. Notably, none of the diameter–triameter properties (even weaker ones) holds for [[Modular graph|modular graphs]], which generalize [[Median graph|median graphs]].
Additionally, one could investigate if [[#D'T|(D<math display="inline">'</math>T)]] or [[#TD'|(TD<math display="inline">'</math>)]] hold for [[Median graph|median graphs]].
* Can better lower '''triameter''' bounds be established in terms of the maximum <math display="inline">\Delta(G)</math> and minimum degree <math display="inline">\sigma(G)</math>?{{R|Das2021}}
